[100 AD | 400 den | you:2000 hr | sch 0 art 0 | rep 5] > policy:
  auto bribe: False
  auto buy people: False
  auto commission: False
  auto forest: False
  auto hire: False
  auto manumit: False
  auto mine: False
  auto mothball: True
  auto open: False
  auto shed: False
  auto train: False
changed: (none)
what each does:
  auto hire: grow the staff toward what you can house and pay
  auto buy people: buy slaves when the workshop is short-handed
  auto manumit: free people you hold, over time
  auto train: teach trades this society does not have when a project needs them
  auto mine: sink a mine when a mineral is holding work up
  auto forest: buy coppice when charcoal is holding work up
  auto mothball: stop working mines you cannot pay for
  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.

[100 AD | 400 den | you:2000 hr | sch 0 art 0 | rep 5] > policy:
  auto bribe: False
  auto buy people: False
  auto commission: False
  auto forest: False
  auto hire: False
  auto manumit: False
  auto mine: False
  auto mothball: True
  auto open: True
  auto shed: False
  auto train: False
changed:
  auto open: True
what each does:
  auto hire: grow the staff toward what you can house and pay
  auto buy people: buy slaves when the workshop is short-handed
  auto manumit: free people you hold, over time
  auto train: teach trades this society does not have when a project needs them
  auto mine: sink a mine when a mineral is holding work up
  auto forest: buy coppice when charcoal is holding work up
  auto mothball: stop working mines you cannot pay for
  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.

[100 AD | -617 den | you:650 hr | sch 0 art 0 | rep 5] > policy:
  auto bribe: False
  auto buy people: False
  auto commission: False
  auto forest: False
  auto hire: False
  auto manumit: False
  auto mine: False
  auto mothball: True
  auto open: False
  auto shed: False
  auto train: False
changed: (none)
what each does:
  auto hire: grow the staff toward what you can house and pay
  auto buy people: buy slaves when the workshop is short-handed
  auto manumit: free people you hold, over time
  auto train: teach trades this society does not have when a project needs them
  auto mine: sink a mine when a mineral is holding work up
  auto forest: buy coppice when charcoal is holding work up
  auto mothball: stop working mines you cannot pay for
  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.

[IN PROGRESS] Third century crisis
  Rome's baseline shifts in what this society values note that it is magic,
  not heterodoxy, that is criminal here, because the state has never before
  needed everyone to worship the same way. The Decian edict of 250 breaks
  that: for the first time, sacrifice to the emperor's genius is demanded
  empire-wide and certified in writing, a loyalty test with no precedent,
  followed by Valerian's edicts against Christians in 257-258. That is a real
  tightening of religious rigidity, not merely more of the old
  magic-suspicion, so it is modelled as its own small shift below rather than
  folded into how readily an inexplicable effect is called sorcery.
  sack chance: you take 100% of it
    what would help: walls, firearms, powerful friends, and copies of your work kept somewhere else
    you could begin now: mil_artillery_piece (9,064, a step toward angled bastion walls no ram or ladder answers)
    academy_network is one of them, waiting on: missing prerequisites: corpus_dispersed, endowment_land
    endowment_land is one of them, waiting on: missing prerequisites: school_founded
  output factor: you take 72% of it (softened by power that does not come by ship, your own roads)
  sack chance after what you have built: 16%
[IN PROGRESS] Currency debasement
  real erosion: you take 100% of it
    what would help: metal you dug yourself, land, and a way to prove what a coin contains
    you could begin now: fin_bimetallism (53.5, a standard the coin can be held to), met_fire_assay (103.9, you can assay ore and coin yourself)
    endowment_land is one of them, waiting on: missing prerequisites: school_founded
    fin_assay_office is one of them, waiting on: missing prerequisites: fin_standard_weights
[284-305] Diocletian's reforms and the Price Edict
  Diocletian came to power in 284 and rebuilt the state by making it much
  heavier. The tetrarchy of 293 gave the empire four courts to feed; the army
  was roughly doubled; the iugatio-capitatio assessment taxed land and heads
  together, often in kind, and needed a census machinery Rome had never had.
  The Edict on Maximum Prices of 301 fixed ceilings on more than a thousand
  goods and wages on pain of death, and Lactantius (De mortibus persecutorum
  7) says blood was shed over trifles until the law was quietly let die. The
  same decades made the collegia hereditary: a man's son inherited his trade
  and could not leave it, which is a direct constraint on anyone who wants to
  work at something new. That, and not the persecution of 303-311, is why how
  much trade is honoured falls here. The state also gets stronger and its
  favour correspondingly more decisive, which is the patronage shift.
  output factor: you take 72% of it (softened by power that does not come by ship, your own roads)
[312-375] The solidus and the end of the debasement
  The debasement modelled above stops, and it is worth saying why, because a
  century of worthless coin is the largest single thing that happened to this
  civilization's money and its end is not a small event. Aurelian reformed the
  antoninianus in 274; Constantine then struck the solidus at 72 to the pound
  of gold from about 309, and it held that weight essentially unchanged for
  seven hundred years. Long contracts, banking and long-distance trade become
  possible again for anyone who can get gold. The other half of this entry is
  quieter and better attested than it is famous: the conquests that supplied
  cheap slaves had ended, the colonate was binding tenants to the land
  instead, and late antiquity is when water power actually spreads in the
  Roman world. Ausonius, writing about the Moselle around 370 (Mosella, lines
  361-364), describes water-driven saws cutting stone - the first securely
  attested water-powered saws anywhere. Rome's baseline hostility to
  labour-saving devices is real but it is at its weakest here, so how a device
  that replaces a man is received moves back toward neutral. This entry
  carries no damage: it is a good century and is modelled as one.
[313-400] Christianisation of the empire
  Rome's baseline note says it is magic and not heterodoxy that is criminal
  here, because the state has never needed everyone to worship the same way.
  Over this century that stops being true. The Edict of Milan in 313 tolerates
  Christianity; Constantius II's law of 357 (Theodosian Code 9.16.4) makes
  consulting a haruspex a capital offence; Theodosius' edict of 380 makes
  Nicene Christianity the religion of the state and the laws of 391-392 close
  the temples and ban sacrifice outright; and in 385 Priscillian is executed
  at Trier, the first man in the empire put to death for holding the wrong
  doctrine. Divination and astrology were already suspect; what is new is that
  there is now one correct answer about the world, and an apparatus for
  finding out who does not hold it. This is the largest single shifts in what
  this society values shift in this file and it runs against the technologist,
  not with him.
[376-405] Adrianople and the Gothic settlement
  Valens let the Tervingi cross the Danube in 376 to escape the Huns,
  mishandled feeding them, and lost two thirds of the eastern field army and
  his own life at Adrianople on 9 August 378; Ammianus (31.13) calls it the
  worst defeat since Cannae. The treaty of 382 then settled the Goths on
  imperial soil under their own leaders, which had never been done before. The
  damage to a workshop is not the battle but what follows it: an army that has
  to be rebuilt is paid for out of taxation, and a frontier that is now inside
  the frontier keeps moving.
